steps.text: The **queen** moves like a rook and a bishop in one piece. She slides any distance along a rank or a file, and any distance along a diagonal, over empty squares. That makes eight directions. The boards next to this card show what you just tried.

steps.caption: From d4 the queen has eight lines and 27 squares. Nothing is in her way.
Put a rook on d4 instead: the straight lines only, 14 squares. That is the first half of the queen.
A bishop on d4: the diagonals only, 13 squares. And 14 plus 13 is 27, so the queen is exactly a rook and a bishop added together.
The queen needs two moves to go from a1 to h5. The kings are only here to make the position legal.

line.say: First a diagonal slide, like a bishop, to the middle of the board.
Black's king just steps aside. We are only watching the queen.
Then a slide along the fifth rank, like a rook. Two moves joined two squares that share no line.

claims.statement: The queen can go from a1 to e5 along the diagonal.
h5 is not on any line from a1, so one move is not enough.

steps.caption: A white pawn stands on d6. The queen can stop on d5, but not on d6 and not beyond it.
A black pawn on d7. The queen may land on d7 and take it, and then her line ends there. She cannot reach d8.

line.say: She lands on the enemy pawn and takes it off the board. A capture ends the slide.

steps.caption: Four black pawns. She can take c5 and d7. The pawn on b6 hides behind c5 on the same diagonal, and e6 is on none of her lines.

steps.text: **When it holds:** on each of her eight lines she slides until something stops her. Her own piece stops her one square early. An enemy piece can be taken, and then she stops on it. **When it fails:** she cannot jump over anything, and she cannot make the knight's L-shaped jump (the knight comes in a later lesson).

steps.caption: Her own pawn on d5 shuts the line upwards. The other seven lines are untouched, so she still has 23 squares.

steps.caption: Why the queen matters. One move to a4 gives check and attacks the rook on a8 at once.

line.say: Check along the diagonal, and the rook on a8 is attacked up the a-file.
Black's king steps aside; nothing can save the rook.
The queen takes the rook with check.

steps.text: Because she reaches so far, the queen can attack two things at once, as here. By convention she is worth about nine pawns, more than a rook (five). [I] Practical advice that follows, our inference rather than a measured rule: do not trade her carelessly, and be wary of bringing her out early where smaller pieces can chase her.

**Rule of thumb, for tapping squares.** Take one of her eight lines at a time. Walk away from her square one step at a time. Stop before your own piece. Stop on the first enemy piece, counting that square. Stop at the edge. Then move to the next line, and finish all eight before you tap.

[H] My guess, not a measured fact: because the queen has so many lines, a beginner's queen mistakes are more often a forgotten diagonal than a forgotten rule. If so, it may help to vary the order in which you check her lines. Notice in the next round which of her lines you looked at last.

steps.prompt: Say it back. In two sentences, explain to a friend how the queen moves and what stops her. The model answer comes next.

steps.text: **Compare.** A model answer: the queen moves like a rook and a bishop together, any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal. She stops before her own pieces and can take the first enemy piece on a line, but never jumps. A blocker on one line leaves her other lines free.
